etymology: Hebrew Dothan; a town north of Shechem, the place where Joseph was sold and where Elisha was surrounded by horses and chariots of fire.
biblical_def: Dothan was a town in the hill country north of Shechem, the setting of two memorable scenes of God's hidden providence. There Joseph, sent by his father to seek his brothers, found them at Dothan, and there they stripped him, cast him into a pit, and sold him to the Ishmaelites bound for Egypt (Gen 37:17-28) — the cruel act by which God, unseen, began to send a deliverer ahead of His people. Centuries later, Dothan was the home of the prophet Elisha when the king of Syria, learning that the prophet revealed his war-plans to Israel, sent a great host by night to seize him; "and they came by night, and compassed the city about" (2 Kgs 6:14). Elisha's servant rose to see the city surrounded and cried out in fear; but Elisha prayed, "LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha" (2 Kgs 6:17). Dothan stands in the dictionary as the place of unseen providence and unseen armies, a witness that God works His saving purpose through the malice of men, and that His people are guarded by hosts the natural eye cannot see, so that "they that be with us are more than they that be with them."
webster_summary: A town north of Shechem where Joseph was sold by his brothers (Gen 37:17) and where Elisha, surrounded by the Syrian host, prayed and his servant saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kgs 6:13-17).

The home of Elisha, surrounded by a Syrian host sent to seize him (2 Kgs 6:13-14).
Where Elisha prayed and his servant's eyes were opened.
Where the mountain was seen full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kgs 6:17).

And he answered, Fear not: for they that be with us are more than they that be with them.

And Elisha prayed, and said, LORD, I pray thee, open his eyes, that he may see. And the LORD opened the eyes of the young man; and he saw: and, behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire round about Elisha.
The angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him, and delivereth them.
corruption_summary: Dothan needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the hidden providence that works good through men's malice, and the unseen armies of God that guard His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Providence-blind correction. To the natural eye, Joseph's sale at Dothan was sheer cruelty and loss; in truth God was sending a savior ahead to preserve life, as Joseph later confessed, "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good" (Gen 50:20). The dictionary holds that God works His saving purposes even through the sins of men, overruling malice for mercy; the believer, like Joseph, may not see the design in the pit, but the hand of God is at work in the darkest providence.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the reality of the unseen armies of God. Elisha's servant saw only the surrounding enemy until God opened his eyes to the mountain full of fiery horses and chariots. The dictionary commends this faith: the people of God are guarded by hosts the natural eye cannot see, "the angel of the LORD encampeth round about them that fear him" (Psa 34:7), and they that be with us are more than they that be with them, however the visible odds may appear.
roots_summary: A town north of Shechem where Joseph was sold (Gen 37:17) and where Elisha's servant saw the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire (2 Kgs 6:13-17).

etymology: Hebrew Ramoth Gilad, "heights of Gilead"; a city of refuge east of the Jordan, long contested with Syria.
biblical_def: Ramoth-gilead was an important city in the highlands of Gilead, east of the Jordan, appointed as a city of refuge and a Levitical city (Deut 4:43; Josh 20:8), and long a point of conflict between Israel and Syria. It is remembered chiefly for two royal events. First, King Ahab of Israel, allied with Jehoshaphat of Judah, went up to retake Ramoth-gilead from Syria against the warning of the prophet Micaiah, who foresaw Israel scattered "as sheep that have not a shepherd"; Ahab disguised himself, but "a certain man drew a bow at a venture, and smote the king of Israel," and he died, exactly as the word of the LORD had said (1 Kgs 22:29-37). Second, it was at Ramoth-gilead, during a later campaign against Syria, that Elisha sent a young prophet to anoint Jehu king over Israel, commissioning him to cut off the house of Ahab (2 Kgs 9:1-6). Ramoth-gilead stands in the dictionary as the contested height where the word of the LORD was vindicated against a king's presumption, and where the LORD raised up Jehu to execute His judgment, a witness that no disguise can hide from God's decree and that He orders the rise and fall of kings according to His sovereign word.
webster_summary: A city of refuge in Gilead, long contested with Syria; where Ahab fell retaking it against Micaiah's warning (1 Kgs 22), and where Elisha had Jehu anointed king over Israel (2 Kgs 9).

Where Ahab was slain by an arrow shot "at a venture" (1 Kgs 22:34).
Where Elisha had Jehu anointed king over Israel (2 Kgs 9:1-6).

There is no wisdom nor understanding nor counsel against the LORD.
corruption_summary: Ramoth-gilead needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are that no presumption or disguise escapes the decreed word of God, and that He sovereignly raises up and casts down kings.
corruption_paragraphs: Presumption correction. Ahab went up to Ramoth-gilead against the clear word of the prophet, trusting his disguise to cheat the decree of God; an arrow shot at random found the gap in his armor. The dictionary holds that there is no wisdom nor counsel against the LORD (Prov 21:30); no stratagem can evade His word, and the man who presumes against a clear warning from God walks knowingly to his ruin, for the word of the LORD stands sure.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is God's sovereign ordering of rulers. At Ramoth-gilead the LORD both ended Ahab's reign and, in another hour, raised up Jehu by anointing to judge Ahab's house. The dictionary holds that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men, setting up and removing kings according to His purpose (Dan 2:21); the thrones of the earth rise and fall not by chance or mere human power, but by the decree of the God who governs all.

etymology: Hebrew Beth Shemesh, "house of the sun"; a Levitical town of Judah where the ark returned from the Philistines.
biblical_def: Beth-shemesh ("house of the sun") was a Levitical town in the lowland of Judah, near the Philistine border, remembered chiefly as the place where the ark of God returned to Israel after its captivity among the Philistines. When the Philistines, plagued by God for keeping the ark, sent it back on a new cart drawn by two milk cows, the cows went straight to Beth-shemesh, lowing as they went, proving the plagues had been from the hand of the LORD; the men of Beth-shemesh, reaping in the valley, rejoiced and offered the cattle as a burnt offering (1 Sam 6:12-15). But there followed a solemn judgment: certain men looked irreverently into the ark, and God struck them, "and the people lamented, because the LORD had smitten many of the people with a great slaughter" (1 Sam 6:19), so that they cried, "Who is able to stand before this holy LORD God?" Beth-shemesh was also where King Amaziah of Judah was defeated and captured by Joash of Israel (2 Kgs 14:11-13). Beth-shemesh stands in the dictionary as the place of the ark's return and a fearful lesson in holy reverence, a witness that the presence of God is not to be treated lightly or pried into with irreverent curiosity, for the LORD is holy, and will be sanctified in them that come near Him.
webster_summary: A Levitical town of Judah where the ark returned from the Philistines on a cart (1 Sam 6); men were struck for looking irreverently into it, a fearful lesson in the holiness of God's presence.

corruption_summary: Beth-shemesh needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the holiness of God's presence, which is not to be treated lightly or pried into with irreverent familiarity.
corruption_paragraphs: Irreverence correction. A casual age approaches God with breezy familiarity, presuming on His grace and prying into holy things. The men of Beth-shemesh, looking irreverently into the ark, learned that the LORD is holy and will not be trifled with. The dictionary holds that God is to be approached with reverence and godly fear (Heb 12:28); His grace invites us near, but never licenses irreverence, and the nearer we come to the holy God, the more reverent, not the more casual, we should be.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the joy and the fear that together belong to God's presence. Beth-shemesh shows both: the people rejoiced at the ark's return and offered sacrifice, yet trembled at His holiness when judgment fell. The dictionary commends this whole-souled response: the believer rejoices in the nearness of God his Savior, and at the same time fears Him as holy, serving Him with gladness and reverence together, for our God is a consuming fire.
roots_summary: A Levitical town of Judah where the ark returned from the Philistines (1 Sam 6); men were struck for looking irreverently into it, a lesson in the holiness of God's presence.

etymology: Hebrew Beth Horon, "house of the hollow"; twin towns (upper and lower) on a strategic pass, where the LORD cast down hailstones on the fleeing Amorites.
biblical_def: Beth-horon was the name of two towns, Upper and Lower Beth-horon, guarding a strategic ascent between the coastal plain and the hill country, the scene of one of the LORD's great victories in Joshua's conquest. When five Amorite kings attacked Gibeon for making peace with Israel, Joshua marched all night and fell upon them; the LORD discomfited them, "and chased them along the way that goeth up to Bethhoron, and smote them to Azekah" (Josh 10:10-11). As they fled down the descent of Beth-horon, "the LORD cast down great stones from heaven upon them... and they died: they were more which died with hailstones than they whom the children of Israel slew with the sword." It was on that day that Joshua commanded the sun to stand still over Gibeon. Beth-horon remained a strategic pass through the history of Israel, and Solomon fortified the towns (1 Kgs 9:17). Beth-horon stands in the dictionary as the place of the LORD's hailstones, a witness that Israel's victories were the LORD's own work, that He fights for His people with the very forces of creation, and that more were slain by the hand of heaven than by the sword of men, that the glory might be plainly God's.
webster_summary: Twin towns on a strategic pass where, in Joshua's conquest, the LORD cast down great hailstones on the fleeing Amorites, killing more than the sword did (Josh 10:10-11); a witness that the victory was God's own work.

corruption_summary: Beth-horon needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is that the LORD fights for His people with the forces of creation, so that the glory of victory is His.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-won-victory correction. The natural pride of man claims the credit for victory. Beth-horon strips it away: more of the enemy died by God's hailstones than by Israel's sword. The dictionary holds that the battles of God's people are the LORD's, and He often so works that no flesh may glory; Israel marched and struck, but it was the hand of heaven that decided the day, that the praise might be plainly God's and not man's.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD fights for His people. He marshaled the very hail of heaven against the Amorites, as He had drowned Pharaoh in the sea. The dictionary commends the faith of Exodus 14:14, "The LORD shall fight for you, and ye shall hold your peace": the people of God are called to obedience and courage, but the victory is His, won by powers no enemy can resist, and theirs is to trust the God who fights for them.

etymology: Hebrew Baal Peratsim, "lord of breakings-through"; where David defeated the Philistines as God broke forth like a flood.
biblical_def: Baal-perazim was the place where King David, newly made king over all Israel, won his first great victory over the Philistines who had come up to seek him. David did not presume but inquired of the LORD, "Shall I go up to the Philistines? wilt thou deliver them into mine hand?" and the LORD said, "Go up: for I will doubtless deliver the Philistines into thine hand" (2 Sam 5:19). David came and smote them, and said, "The LORD hath broken forth upon mine enemies before me, as the breach of waters. Therefore he called the name of that place Baalperazim" (2 Sam 5:20) — the place of breakings-through, for God had burst upon the enemy like a flood breaking through a dam. The prophet Isaiah later recalled this victory, saying the LORD would rise up "as in mount Perazim" to do His work (Isa 28:21). Baal-perazim stands in the dictionary as the place where God broke through like a flood, a witness to the blessing of inquiring of the LORD before battle, to the truth that victory comes from God who Himself breaks the power of the enemy, and to the readiness of God to burst forth in power for His people when they seek Him and obey.
webster_summary: Where David, having inquired of the LORD, defeated the Philistines; he named it Baal-perazim ("lord of breakings-through") because "the LORD hath broken forth upon mine enemies... as the breach of waters" (2 Sam 5:20).

corruption_summary: Baal-perazim needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the blessing of seeking the LORD before acting, and the power of God who breaks through like a flood for His people.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-reliant action correction. The impulse of the flesh is to act first and seek God after. David, though a seasoned warrior and now king, inquired of the LORD before going up, and received both command and promise. The dictionary holds the wisdom of seeking God before battle: the believer is to acknowledge the LORD in all his ways, that He may direct his paths (Prov 3:6), and the victories that begin in prayerful inquiry of God are crowned with His blessing.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God Himself breaks the power of the enemy. David did not boast that he had broken through, but that "the LORD hath broken forth upon mine enemies... as the breach of waters." The dictionary commends this confession: the victory belongs to God, who bursts upon the foe with irresistible power, and His people, running through troops and leaping walls, do so only by their God (Psa 18:29), to whom alone the praise is due.

etymology: Hebrew Ophrah; the town of the Abiezrites, home of Gideon, where the angel of the LORD called him and he built the altar Jehovah-shalom.
biblical_def: Ophrah was the home town of Gideon, of the family of the Abiezrites in the tribe of Manasseh, the setting of his calling and of both his great obedience and his later failure. There the angel of the LORD appeared to Gideon as he threshed wheat in secret for fear of the Midianites, greeting him, "The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour" (Judg 6:12), and commissioning him to deliver Israel. When the LORD met his fears with the assurance of peace, Gideon "built an altar there unto the LORD, and called it Jehovahshalom: ... it is yet in Ophrah of the Abiezrites" (Judg 6:24) — "the LORD is peace." At Ophrah, too, Gideon tore down his father's altar of Baal and the grove, earning the name Jerubbaal. Yet Ophrah also witnessed Gideon's later folly: after his victories, he made an ephod of the gold of the spoil and set it there, "and all Israel went thither a whoring after it: which thing became a snare unto Gideon, and to his house" (Judg 8:27). Ophrah stands in the dictionary as the town of Gideon's calling and his snare, a witness both to the God who calls the fearful to valour and meets them with peace, and to the danger that even a great deliverer may, by an unwise device, lead the people he saved back into idolatry.
webster_summary: The home of Gideon (Judg 6-8), where the angel of the LORD called him and he built the altar Jehovah-shalom ("the LORD is peace"); later the site of the ephod that became a snare to Israel.

corruption_summary: Ophrah needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the God who calls the fearful to valour and gives peace, and the danger that even a deliverer may, by an unwise device, become a snare.
corruption_paragraphs: Self-sufficiency correction. Gideon was a fearful man threshing in secret when God called him "mighty man of valour" — not for what he was, but for what God would make him. The dictionary holds that God's call creates the strength it commands; He chooses the weak and fearful, meets their dread with His peace (Jehovah-shalom), and makes them mighty by His presence, that the deliverance may be seen to be His.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the peril of the godly man's later folly. The same Gideon who tore down Baal's altar at Ophrah later set up an ephod there that ensnared Israel in idolatry. The dictionary commends the warning of 1 Corinthians 10:12, "let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall": past faithfulness is no guarantee against future folly, and even great servants of God must watch and pray, lest an unwise device of their own become a snare to themselves and to those they lead.

etymology: Hebrew Ziph; a town and wilderness in the hill country of Judah where David hid from Saul and was twice betrayed by the Ziphites.
biblical_def: Ziph was a town and surrounding wilderness in the hill country of Judah, south of Hebron, a chief refuge of David during his long flight from King Saul. There, "in a wood" in the wilderness of Ziph, David hid; and there came to him his friend Jonathan, who "strengthened his hand in God" (1 Sam 23:16), assuring him that he would yet be king and renewing their covenant — one of the tenderest scenes of faithful friendship in Scripture. But the men of Ziph twice betrayed David's hiding-place to Saul, saying, "Doth not David hide himself with us?" (1 Sam 23:19; 26:1), sending the king to hunt him. It was during this Ziphite pursuit that David, finding Saul asleep in the camp, refused to harm the LORD's anointed, taking only his spear and cruse of water, and called out his innocence across the valley (1 Sam 26). Psalm 54 is titled as written "when the Ziphites came and said to Saul, Doth not David hide himself with us?" Ziph stands in the dictionary as the wilderness of David's hiding and betrayal, a witness to the strengthening power of a faithful friend who points the weary to God, to the grief of being betrayed by one's own countrymen, and to the grace by which David, though hunted and handed over, would not lift his hand against the anointed but committed his cause to God.
webster_summary: A wilderness in Judah where David hid from Saul; there Jonathan "strengthened his hand in God" (1 Sam 23:16), but the Ziphites twice betrayed his hiding-place to Saul; the setting of Psalm 54.

corruption_summary: Ziph needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are the ministry of a friend who strengthens the hand in God, the grief of betrayal, and the grace that refuses to avenge itself.
corruption_paragraphs: Friendless-faith correction. The lonely and hunted are tempted to despair. Into David's wilderness came Jonathan, who "strengthened his hand in God" — not with mere sympathy, but by pointing him to the LORD and His promise. The dictionary holds the high ministry of godly friendship: to strengthen a weary brother's hand in God, to remind him of God's faithfulness when his own heart fails, is a precious and needed service, and the friend who does it does the work of God.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is committing one's cause to God rather than avenging oneself. Betrayed by the Ziphites and hunted by Saul, David twice spared the king who sought his life, refusing to stretch out his hand against the LORD's anointed and leaving his vindication to God. The dictionary commends his restraint: the wronged believer is not to take vengeance, but to commit himself "to him that judgeth righteously" (1 Pet 2:23), confident, with Psalm 54, that God is his helper and will uphold his soul.

Jonathan... strengthened his hand in God (1 Sam 23:16) — the ministry of a faithful friend.

etymology: Hebrew Tsoar, "little"; the small city of the plain to which Lot fled and which was spared at his request.
biblical_def: Zoar was one of the cities of the plain near the Salt Sea, originally called Bela, the small town to which Lot fled when God rained fire and brimstone upon Sodom and Gomorrah. As the angels urged Lot to escape to the mountain, he begged instead to flee to a nearby little city: "Behold now, this city is near to flee unto, and it is a little one... is it not a little one? and my soul shall live" (Gen 19:20). The LORD granted his plea: "I have accepted thee concerning this thing also, that I will not overthrow this city... Therefore the name of the city was called Zoar" (Gen 19:21-22) — "little." Indeed, the angel said he could do nothing until Lot had come there; the rescue of one righteous man held back the judgment until he was safe. Yet Lot, who had begged for Zoar, soon feared to dwell there and went up into the mountain to live in a cave (Gen 19:30). Zoar stands in the dictionary as the little city of refuge spared for Lot's sake, a witness to the mercy of God who hears the prayers of the weak and delivers the righteous from judgment, and a sober picture of Lot himself, whose worldly choices had so impoverished his faith that he scarcely knew where to find rest even in the mercy God granted him.
webster_summary: The small city of the plain ("little") to which Lot fled from Sodom and which God spared at his plea (Gen 19:20-22); a witness to God's mercy in delivering the righteous from judgment.

The Lord knoweth how to deliver the godly out of temptations, and to reserve the unjust unto the day of judgment to be punished:
corruption_summary: Zoar needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are God's mercy in delivering the righteous before judgment falls, and the impoverished faith of Lot, whose worldly choices left him weak even in his rescue.
corruption_paragraphs: Mercy-doubted correction. Some imagine God deaf to the prayers of the weak and faltering. Lot, frightened and faltering, begged for the little city, and God granted it, even holding back the fire until His servant was safe. The dictionary holds that the Lord knows how to deliver the godly out of temptation (2 Pet 2:9); He hears the trembling prayers of weak believers, and the rescue of even one righteous man may stay the falling of judgment until he is safe.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the impoverishing cost of worldly choices. Lot, who had once pitched his tent toward Sodom for its good land, was so weakened by his worldliness that he could scarcely find rest even in the mercy God granted, begging for Zoar and then fearing to stay there. The dictionary commends the warning: the believer who makes his home among the wicked for worldly gain may be saved, yet so as by fire, his faith impoverished and his life barren, a righteous man with little to show for his years.

etymology: Hebrew Luz, perhaps "almond tree"; the original Canaanite name of the place Jacob renamed Bethel after his vision of the ladder.
biblical_def: Luz was the original name of the place that Jacob renamed Bethel after his vision of the heavenly ladder. Fleeing from Esau toward Haran, Jacob lay down for the night in a certain place and dreamed of a ladder set up between earth and heaven, the angels of God ascending and descending on it, and the LORD standing above it renewing the covenant promise: "I am the LORD God of Abraham thy father... in thee and in thy seed shall all the families of the earth be blessed" (Gen 28:13-14). Awaking in awe, Jacob said, "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not... this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven"; he set up the stone as a pillar and "called the name of that place Bethel: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first" (Gen 28:19). Bethel, "house of God," thus replaced the old name Luz. Luz stands in the dictionary as the former name of Bethel, a witness to the transforming encounter with God that turns an ordinary, unnamed place into the house of God and the gate of heaven, and a reminder that the LORD meets His pilgrims in unexpected places, renewing His covenant and turning a stone of the field into a memorial of His grace.
webster_summary: The original Canaanite name of Bethel, renamed by Jacob after his vision of the ladder between earth and heaven (Gen 28:19); a witness to the encounter with God that makes an ordinary place "the house of God."

scriptures: And Jacob awaked out of his sleep, and he said, Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not.
And he was afraid, and said, How dreadful is this place! this is none other but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven.
And he called the name of that place Bethel: but the name of that city was called Luz at the first.
...Hereafter ye shall see heaven open, and the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man.
corruption_summary: Luz needs no defense from redefinition; its lesson is the transforming encounter with God that makes an ordinary place the house of God, fulfilled in Christ, the true ladder between heaven and earth.
corruption_paragraphs: God-confined correction. Jacob supposed God belonged to certain holy places and was surprised to meet Him in an unnamed waste: "Surely the LORD is in this place; and I knew it not." The dictionary holds that God is not confined to temples or shrines; He meets His pilgrims in unexpected places, and any spot where He reveals Himself becomes, for that soul, the house of God and the gate of heaven. The encounter, not the geography, makes the place holy.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is Christ as the true ladder of Bethel. The Lord Jesus applied Jacob's vision to Himself, promising His disciples they would see "the angels of God ascending and descending upon the Son of man" (John 1:51). The dictionary commends this fulfillment: Christ is the true and living way between heaven and earth, the one Mediator by whom alone sinners ascend to God and God's blessing descends to men; in Him every believing soul finds the house of God and the gate of heaven.

etymology: Hebrew Rabbah, "great"; the royal city of the Ammonites, besieged while David sinned with Bathsheba.
biblical_def: Rabbah was the chief royal city of the Ammonites, east of the Jordan, whose siege forms the dark backdrop of David's great sin. While David's army under Joab besieged Rabbah, "David tarried still at Jerusalem" (2 Sam 11:1), and there, idle when he should have been at war, he fell into adultery with Bathsheba and then engineered the death of her husband Uriah, who was killed before the walls of Rabbah by David's own command, carried in a letter by Uriah's own hand (2 Sam 11:14-17). The siege ground on until Joab, having taken the city's water-defenses, summoned David to come and complete the conquest, lest the city be called by Joab's name; David came, took the city and its great crown of gold, and brought out its people to hard labor (2 Sam 12:26-31). Rabbah was later denounced by the prophets for the cruelty of the Ammonites (Amos 1:14; Jer 49:2-3). Rabbah stands in the dictionary as the city before whose walls Uriah died and David sinned, a sober witness that idleness in the place of duty opens the door to grievous sin, that the powerful may use even the engines of war to cover their crimes, and that the God who sees brings the hidden sins of His servants into the light.
webster_summary: The royal city of the Ammonites besieged by Joab while David, idle at Jerusalem, sinned with Bathsheba and had Uriah killed before its walls (2 Sam 11-12); a sober backdrop to David's great fall.

scriptures: And he wrote in the letter, saying, Set ye Uriah in the forefront of the hottest battle, and retire ye from him, that he may be smitten, and die.
Wherefore hast thou despised the commandment of the LORD, to do evil in his sight? thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword...
...behold, ye have sinned against the LORD: and be sure your sin will find you out.
corruption_summary: Rabbah needs no defense from redefinition; its lessons are that idleness in the place of duty opens the door to sin, and that the hidden crimes of the powerful do not escape the God who sees.
corruption_paragraphs: Idleness correction. "At the time when kings go forth to battle... David tarried still at Jerusalem," and the idle hour became the occasion of adultery and murder. The dictionary holds the danger of idleness in the place of duty: when the servant of God abandons his post and his work, he exposes himself to temptations he would not meet in faithful labor. David's fall began not with the sin but with the staying home; the safest place is the place of duty.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that sin will find the sinner out, however powerful he be. David used the siege of Rabbah and a sealed letter to cover his crime, hiding murder behind the chances of war; but the LORD saw, and sent Nathan to say, "thou hast killed Uriah the Hittite with the sword" (2 Sam 12:9). The dictionary commends the warning of Numbers 32:23, "be sure your sin will find you out": no rank, secrecy, or stratagem hides sin from God, who brings the hidden things to light and calls even kings to account.
